author: José Siles
headline: AI Engineer at Nestlé | LinkedIn Instructor | +165k AI Community | Trusted by +50 Global Brands
text:
Finding duplicates is a daily task in SQL.

But the way you find them depends entirely on what you plan to do next:

Do you just need a count?
Are you trying to delete the extras?
Do you need to compare the conflicting rows side-by-side?

Here are 3 powerful ways to find duplicates in SQL:

1️⃣ 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗨𝗣 𝗕𝗬 + 𝗛𝗔𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗚 ⮕ The Counter

This is the quickest way to see which keys have problems and how bad the duplication is. It’s the "bird's-eye view."

2️⃣ 𝗥𝗢𝗪_𝗡𝗨𝗠𝗕𝗘𝗥() ⮕ The Cleaner

Perfect for deduplication. By ranking occurrences, you can easily isolate the "extra" rows (WHERE rn > 1).

3️⃣𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗙 𝗝𝗢𝗜𝗡 ⮕ The Comparator

Great for deeper analysis. It shows you the conflicting pairs side-by-side so you can investigate exactly why they matched.

Down below you'll find the SQL implementation 👇🏻

Which method do you find yourself using most often?

I normally start with the first method for the initial iteration, and then move to the second for deduplication.

🚀 SQL Query Optimization: 10x Faster Performance

Dealing with slow-running queries? Here are 6 powerful techniques that can instantly elevate your database performance:
 ✅ Use Indexes Wisely — Achieve up to 90% faster lookups
 ✅ Select Only What You Need — Cut unnecessary I/O by 50%
 ✅ Choose EXISTS Over IN — 70% speed boost for large subqueries
 ✅ Tune Your JOINs — Get up to 80% improvement with proper indexing
 ✅ Filter Early — Apply WHERE before aggregates for 60% faster execution
 ✅ Avoid Functions on Indexed Columns — Preserve index range scans (85% faster)

💡 Even adopting just 2–3 of these optimizations can turn response times from seconds into milliseconds.

Smart performance isn’t just about writing SQL—it’s about writing optimized SQL. And when you're working with millions of rows, every millisecond matters.

text:
❌ I failed a SQL interview once because I didn’t know the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(1), COUNT(column), and COUNT(DISTINCT).

I thought they were all the same, but they’re not! Here’s a quick heads-up if you’re learning SQL or prepping for interviews.

- COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) count all rows, including NULLs.
- COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values in that column.
- COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique, non-NULL values, ignoring duplicates.

This small difference saved me from future mistakes and confusion. I use COUNT almost every day now — and you should too!
